Regularity across a distinguished variable

Reconstructed and checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A differential equation can force smooth dependence on time while leaving point masses in space. We prove this for equations monic in the time derivative, with arbitrary differential operators in the transverse variables. The proof uses finite continuous primitives, lowers their number of time derivatives, and then applies the fundamental theorem of calculus in distribution pairings. At an endpoint, the same construction explains exactly what must extend.

All pairings are complex linear. The earlier proofs used below are U008, Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 5.1, for finite-order actions on tests and uniform convergence on bounded smooth test families; U021, B0–B3 and Theorems 1.1–2.1, for localization, gluing and finite-regularity convolution; and U031, Theorem 6.1, for the full mixed continuous-primitive construction, including its finite compact version. Completeness of the support test spaces and the complete-metric Baire theorem are proved in functional foundations, Sections 6 and 14.1–14.2. We prove the required arbitrary-family estimate here.

The full monic equation

What a boundary hypothesis must control

At a finite endpoint, means strong continuity of the derivatives through order , with the derivatives defined one-sidedly there. No condition is imposed at an infinite endpoint.

Example 4.1 (extendible distributions with a divergent trace). On and , put and . Then . The forcing extends continuously by zero, and extends distributionally across zero. To check the latter without assuming a principal-value theorem, for a test on an interval containing zero choose inside that interval and write Extend the test by zero when needed. The first integrand has absolute value at most , by the scalar fundamental theorem. On a fixed test support the remaining integral is bounded by a constant times . The formula is therefore a distribution, restricts to for positive , and is denoted . Tensoring it with the constant transverse function gives the extension of , for example to .

Nevertheless, a transverse test of integral one pairs with as , so there is no distributional trace at zero. The coefficient fails to extend smoothly there. Distributional extendibility of the solution alone is insufficient.

Theorem 4.2 (regularity up to a boundary). In Theorem 3.1, suppose the coefficients of all extend smoothly to , where is an open neighbourhood of ; suppose extends as a distribution there; and suppose is continuous on with values in . Then The assertion is local at each finite endpoint. The extended distribution need not satisfy the equation outside .

Proof. Consider the left endpoint ; the right endpoint is identical with reversed one-sided intervals. Differentiate a chosen extension of to form an extension of its companion vector. Cut it off on a product box crossing . U031's finite compact primitive theorem gives (2.4) with finitely many coefficients continuous across , so their restrictions extend continuously to the closed half-box.

On the same one-sided compact time interval, Lemmas 1.1–2.1 give the forcing a representation by transverse derivatives of coefficients continuous up to . These functions can be extended continuously across by their endpoint values. We now perform the reduction of Lemma 2.2 only on the open side , keeping track of continuous endpoint values of every coefficient.

In forming , all coefficient derivatives in (2.2) extend smoothly, and therefore are bounded and continuous on the smaller closed box. Multiplying them by the continuous primitive coefficients preserves continuous endpoint values. The integrals in (2.5), taken from a fixed interior , also have continuous limits at , because their integrands are continuous on a compact half-box. Lemma 1.3 on the interior supplies , whose transverse continuous-primitive representation is independent of time. Thus each reduction lowers the normal degree and preserves continuous extension of the coefficients. Finitely many nested spatial boxes permit all reductions. The final degree-zero representation defines a weakly continuous curve up to , and Lemma 1.2 makes it strongly continuous.

These endpoint curves agree on overlaps: they agree for by interior uniqueness, and their scalar pairings have the same limits at . U021 B0 therefore glues them at the endpoint. The finite test decomposition used in Lemma 2.2 proves continuity of the resulting global curve on .

The right side of the companion system is now continuous on the closed half-interval, by the moving-test estimate in Theorem 3.1. Identity (3.2), initially valid for interior , extends to in every scalar pairing; a common order controls the integral. The same strong average estimate, with at , gives its one-sided derivative . The companion identities then give all one-sided derivatives and their strong continuity. Every equation used in this argument was on the original interior or was its continuous limit.

Traces create boundary sources under zero extension

Proposition 5.1 (all normal derivatives of a zero extension). Let be finite and . Its zero extension is the distribution For , The first term denotes the joint distribution of the restricted curve extended by zero, not a product of arbitrary distributions.

Proof. Lemma 1.1 gives the fixed-support bound for (5.1). For a joint test set . Its scalar pairing obeys To verify this, split the difference quotient as The first term tends to . In the second, the test quotient tends in every derivative norm to ; its error is controlled uniformly by Lemma 1.1, and its fixed limiting test is handled by weak continuity of . The two terms on the resulting right side are continuous, by the same moving-test argument. Scalar integration by parts consequently gives on every joint test. Apply this to and differentiate the two existing endpoint masses. Repeating the step gives exactly the two sums in (5.2). Tensor derivatives are defined by , which also checks every sign.

This specifies one particular extension. Another extension can include distributions supported on the endpoint slices, and need not obey (5.2). For a homogeneous equation, the zero extension must include the displayed boundary forcing unless those terms cancel.
